title: Golden corpus expected-result file
description: Format for tests/fixtures/golden/<case>.expected.json, documented in docs/build-plan.md Phase 1. Validated by tests/test_golden_corpus.py against a small hand-rolled validator (see that file for why this isn't the `jsonschema` package) — this document is the single source of truth either way.

expected_spans.description: Spans a detector is expected to find, in the coordinate system src/sendashield/normalise.py defines. Empty for benign and near-miss fixtures.

detector.description: DETECTOR_ID of the detector expected to find this span. Matches the order in docs/build-plan.md Phase 2. This phase (build-plan Phase 1) only uses credit_card and iban — no detector code exists yet to produce the others.

end.description: Exclusive end offset into normalise(raw_message).text. Must be > start.

text.description: The exact substring normalised_text[start:end] must equal. This is the self-consistency check the golden test enforces.

expected_action.description: The policy action this item should resolve to once a pipeline exists. allow <-> mask <-> quarantine per CLAUDE.md invariant 4 (escalation only) — this field records the target, not an assertion this phase's tests can check yet. Every mail hit fixture is 'mask', which is correct for a single checksum-validated identifier in an otherwise legitimate business message: there is a specific span to replace, so withholding the whole item would be over-masking. The 'quarantine' cases are the two sensitive calendar fixtures, where per architecture.md §5 the sensitivity is the item and not a span — an oncology appointment has no span to replace, and masking the title would leave an empty event that still reveals the appointment happened. Note these declare quarantine with an empty expected_spans, which is correct and not a contradiction: the target action is L3 topic classification (topic_health, topic_hr), and no L1 detector should fire on them. Further quarantine cases arrive with the attachment batch (unscannable content — nothing to mask, so nothing may pass) and the rest of the L3 batch at M4 (parse failure or timeout, which per CLAUDE.md invariant 11 quarantines with no lenient retry). ---- THE RULE FOR INJECTION FIXTURES, which is not obvious and is easy to get backwards: the action keys on the ANOMALY, never on the invisible_stripped transform. Hidden content stripped with nothing suspicious in it is 'allow' — the payload is already gone, so allowing costs no exposure, and display:none preheader text appears in a large share of all marketing and transactional email, so quarantining on the transform alone would withhold most of a normal inbox. That is exactly the over-blocking failure architecture.md §5's action asymmetry exists to prevent. Hidden content stripped PLUS an injection anomaly is 'quarantine' — not because the payload could still reach the model (L0 removed it) but because a message deliberately constructed to manipulate an AI reader is one the user should see for themselves rather than have summarised. benign_hidden_preheader_text is the fixture that pins the allow side of this distinction; the injection_* fixtures pin the quarantine side.

must_not_appear_in_output.description: Literal strings that must never appear in a masked or quarantined item's output. Empty for allow-action fixtures. Each entry must also APPEAR IN THE RAW NORMALISED TEXT of the paired message — test_golden_fixture_is_internally_consistent enforces this, and the check is not redundant with the leak assertion it looks like a duplicate of. Reason: a leak assertion over a string the message never contained passes trivially, forever, while looking exactly like protection. That is the failure mode this project exists to prevent, reproduced inside its own test suite — a fixture would claim to guard a leak that could not occur. Requiring presence in the source makes the assertion falsifiable: the string is there before filtering, so its absence afterwards means filtering did something. Do not remove this constraint as a duplicate of the span check; spans are what a detector should find, this is what must not survive, and a fixture may legitimately declare the second without the first.

expected_stripped.description: Literal strings that L0 invisible-content stripping must REMOVE, so they are absent from the normalised text entirely. The mirror image of must_not_appear_in_output, and checked with the mirror-image integrity rule: each entry must be present in the raw fixture bytes but absent from the normalised text. Requiring presence in the source is what makes the assertion falsifiable — a fixture claiming to strip something the message never contained would pass forever while testing nothing, the same trap must_not_appear_in_output guards against from the other side. Because the check reads the raw bytes, a fixture using expected_stripped must not be base64 or quoted-printable encoded. Optional; omit for fixtures that strip nothing.

expected_anomalies.description: Anomaly labels normalise() must raise for this fixture, per NormalisedText.anomalies. Exact match on the whole set, not a subset: an unexpected anomaly is as much a change in behaviour as a missing one, and a subset check would let a new false positive land unnoticed across the corpus. Labels only, never content — these values reach the audit log. Optional; omit for fixtures that raise none, which is equivalent to declaring an empty list. ---- DO NOT RELAX THIS TO A SUBSET CHECK. Exact matching means that adding a new anomaly type churns every fixture it newly fires on, and that churn will look like pointless busywork at the moment it happens. It is the point. A new anomaly firing across the corpus is precisely the event worth reviewing case by case, because it is either a real signal nobody had noticed or a false positive about to be normalised into the baseline. A subset check makes both invisible and turns this field into a record of what someone once expected rather than what the code does.

notes.description: One-line human-readable description of what the fixture tests and why. Required — this is what a reviewer reads instead of the raw message.
